pedagogy.summary:
- **Age:** 7–8 years

- **Topic:** Contact & Non-Contact Forces

- **Standards — UK (DfE National Curriculum, Year 3 Forces and Magnets):** Notice that some forces need contact between 2 objects, but magnetic forces can act at a distance (non-statutory guidance: magnetic forces can act without direct contact, unlike most forces where direct contact is necessary).

- **Standards — US (NGSS 3-PS2-3):** [curriculum wording omitted; reference 3-PS2-3] (assessment limited to forces produced by objects students can manipulate; electrical interactions limited to static electricity).

- **Operational details:** At 7-8, build the contact vs non-contact distinction from first-hand experience. A force is a push or pull arising from an interaction between two objects. Contact forces (push, pull, friction, air resistance, upthrust) act only when objects touch; non-contact forces (gravity, magnetism, static electricity) act across a gap. Magnetism is the most child-manageable non-contact example — a tactile experience of action without touching. The central conceptual hurdle is that children expect a force to require contact ('how can the Earth pull a ball it isn't touching?'); the IOP stresses teachers should treat action-at-a-distance as genuinely remarkable, not obvious, since it is the start of the journey towards fields.

- **Checkpoint:** Tier A (concrete/observational).
bestPractices: Give first-hand, tactile experience of a non-contact force with real magnets — feel the push/pull across an empty gap before any abstraction
Sort everyday forces into contact / non-contact and surface the rule that distinguishes them: 'do the two objects have to be touching?'
Keep magnetic, gravitational (and electrostatic) forces SEPARATE while noting they share 'act at a distance' behaviour — do not conflate their terminology or representations
Do NOT present action-at-a-distance as obvious; if pupils think it is obvious they are missing the point — honour the strangeness
Use predict-then-test (will the magnet still attract through the table? through a gap?) and discuss the reasoning afterwards
At this age avoid newton-meters, magnetic-field language and iron filings — keep it exploratory and hands-on
keyRepresentations: Two-object interaction picture with an arrow from A to B: 'what is pushing or pulling what?'
Contact / non-contact sorting mat with an explicit 'do they touch?' gap test
Force-word badges (contact vs non-contact) anchored on a familiar scene
commonMisconceptions: Forces must require contact — non-contact action feels impossible ('how can the Earth pull a ball it isn't touching?'); this is the core hurdle

Gravity is caused by magnetism / the Earth is a giant magnet — both act at a distance and are felt at the surface, so children conflate them. Discriminators: gravity ALWAYS attracts and acts on anything with mass; magnetism attracts AND repels and acts only on specific materials (iron, steel, nickel, cobalt)
Non-contact forces 'need air' to travel through — that magnets or gravity would stop working in a vacuum (false; no medium is required)
All metals are magnetic (transfer of 'metal = special' from electricity work)
A force is a property an object 'has' rather than an interaction between two objects

learn.summary: For 7–8 year olds, build the contact vs non-contact force distinction from first-hand experience. A force is a push or pull arising from an interaction between two objects. Contact forces (pushes and pulls made by touching, such as a hand pushing a door, plus friction, air resistance and upthrust) act only when objects touch; non-contact forces (magnetism, gravity, static electricity) act across a gap. Magnetism is the most child-manageable tactile example of action at a distance. The central hurdle is children expecting a force to need contact ('how can the Earth pull a ball it isn't touching?'); treat action-at-a-distance as genuinely remarkable, not obvious. Keep magnetic, gravitational and electrostatic forces separate while noting they share 'act at a distance' behaviour. At this age avoid newton-meters, field language and iron filings.

activities.title: Feel and see the pull across an empty gap
feedback: If you expected an arrow only when the magnet and paperclip touched: look again — the pull-arrow appeared on the paperclip while there was still a gap. That pull across the gap is what makes magnetism a non-contact force.
If you thought the wooden blocks should show an arrow across the gap: the blocks only push or pull when they meet — that makes them a contact interaction, unlike the magnet.
If you thought removing the air would stop the magnet: the pull stayed the same with the air removed — the air is not carrying the force across the gap.
Name what is pushing or pulling what in each case: a force is an interaction between two objects, not something one object simply 'has'.
activities.rationale: A live, state-based model lets the force arrow recompute as the gap opens and closes, making the contrast between gap-spanning and contact-only forces concrete; the 'remove the air' toggle is intended to address the 'needs air' misconception. The hands-on magnet is itself part of the learning, so pair the digital gap-test with real magnets. The linked arrows, live recomputation and air toggle are illustrative mechanisms, not required features — a physical magnet, a sheet slipped into the gap, and spoken prediction can carry the same contrast.
sourceClaims: Magnetism is a child-manageable, tactile example of action without contact; action-at-a-distance should be treated as remarkable not obvious; keep magnetic/electric/gravitational forces separate; early magnet work should avoid newton-meters, fields and iron filings.
learnerActions: Hold a real magnet and a paperclip in your hands and slowly bring them together until you feel the pull before they touch — describe the pull in your own words.

On a drag-and-release scene, move a magnet slowly toward a paperclip across an empty gap and watch a pull-arrow appear on the paperclip, pointing toward the magnet, before they touch, thickening as the gap narrows.
Repeat the same drag with two wooden blocks and notice that NO arrow appears until the blocks actually meet.
Say aloud which force reached across the empty space and which only acted on contact, and name a real-world parallel (the Earth pulling a dropped ball).
Toggle a 'remove the air' control and observe that the magnet's pull is unchanged.
activities.intendedInsight: Some forces (magnetism, and the Earth pulling a ball) act across empty space, while contact forces only act when two objects touch; the pull does not need air in the gap to work.

activities.title: Predict-then-test: what gets through the gap?
feedback: If you predicted the paper would block the pull: that is contact-thinking. The paper fills the gap but the pull still reaches the paperclip, because paper is not a magnetic material and nothing has to bridge the gap for a magnet's pull to act.

If you were surprised the steel tray changed things: that is about material, not about touching. Steel is a magnetic material, so the tray is itself attracted to the magnet — the paperclip may be drawn to the tray, and/or the pull reaching the original paperclip may be reduced or blocked. Paper, which is not magnetic, does none of this. How much happens depends on how thick the tray is and how strong the magnet is, so try it with your own tray and magnet and watch carefully.
If you said removing the air would stop the pull: magnets work in a vacuum and under water too; the air is not carrying the force.
activities.rationale: Predict-then-test surfaces the learner's reasoning and makes the surprise (paper does not block, but a magnetic steel tray interacts with the magnet) the trigger for discussing action-at-a-distance and material-specificity. Discussing the reasoning afterwards is as important as the result; because the tray outcome is setup-dependent, test the specific equipment first.
learnerActions: Set a paperclip a small gap from a magnet and predict whether the pull still works when you slip a sheet of paper into the gap, and explain WHY.
Test it, then predict and test again with a steel baking tray slipped into the gap.
Discuss afterwards: did paper stop the pull? What did the steel tray do? What does that tell you about what the force needs to travel through and what materials it acts on?
Predict what would happen if the magnet and paperclip sat in a jar with all the air sucked out.
activities.intendedInsight: A non-contact force acts across a genuine gap and does not require air as a go-between; the magnet acts only on specific magnetic materials (such as iron, most steels, nickel and cobalt), which is why a magnetic steel tray interacts with the magnet while non-magnetic paper does not.

activities.title: Distinguish gravity from magnetism
feedback: If you grouped gravity and magnetism as the same invisible pull: they share 'acting across a gap', which is why they are easy to confuse, but gravity never repels and pulls every object with mass, while magnetism can repel and only acts on certain metals.
If you expected the magnet to pull the aluminium can: not all metals are magnetic — the magnet acts on iron/steel-type materials, not aluminium.
If you called the dropped ball 'magnetism': the Earth pulls the ball by gravity because the ball has mass; the Earth is not acting as a giant magnet here.
activities.rationale: Children's everyday magnet experience is mostly of attraction, so they do not spontaneously separate magnetism from gravity or static electricity. Offering explicit discriminators (always-attracts vs attract-and-repel; any mass vs specific materials) helps keep the forces distinct without conflating their terminology.
sourceClaims: Gravity and the Earth's magnetic field are independent; a simple distinction is that gravitational forces always attract and never repel, while magnetism acts only on specific materials (mainly iron and certain iron alloys) and can attract and repel. Both act at a distance and are felt at the surface, which is the source of the confusion.

Young children's everyday magnet experiences are mostly of attraction and they do not see the need to discriminate magnetic forces from gravity or electrostatic forces — they appear to be the same invisible non-contact force.
learnerActions: Compare: does the magnet pull an aluminium can the way it pulls a steel paperclip? Try it and say why the difference matters.
State one way gravity and magnetism are alike (for example, both act across a distance without the objects touching) and two ways they differ.
Decide, for a worked example, whether gravity or magnetism is acting: a dropped ball; a magnet picking up a steel pin; a magnet pushing away another magnet.
activities.intendedInsight: Gravity and magnetism both act at a distance but are different forces: gravity ALWAYS attracts and acts on anything with mass; magnetism attracts AND repels (repelling happens between two magnets) and acts only on specific materials (such as iron, most steels, nickel and cobalt).

activities.title: Sort everyday forces and explain the rule
feedback: A correct sort of hand pushes and friction as contact and magnetism as non-contact is a good start — but add WHY: a non-contact force acts across a gap with no air or material needed in between.
If a check answer ties the pull to needing air: magnets work in a vacuum, so the air is not the go-between.

Watch for two common wrong ideas: 'things fall because the Earth is a giant magnet' (the Earth does have magnetism, which is why compasses work, but falling is caused by gravity) and 'the force needs air to travel' — be ready to say why each is wrong.
activities.rationale: Categorising and a short choice task built from the conflation misconceptions make strong retrieval practice once the concept has been met. Recognition and sorting on their own do not themselves elicit an independent explanation, so require a spoken or written reason alongside each placement; this is a consolidation step, not where the idea first clicks.
learnerActions: Drag or place each everyday force (a hand pushing a door, a hand pulling a rope, friction, air resistance, upthrust, magnetism, gravity) into a contact or non-contact category.
After each placement, state the test you used: 'do the two objects have to be touching?'
For a non-contact example, explain in a sentence that the force acts across a gap with no medium needed — do not just name the category.
Answer a short check: would a magnet still pull a paperclip in a vacuum? Why?
activities.intendedInsight: The dividing rule is whether the two objects must touch for the force to act; sorting correctly plus explaining the gap-spanning behaviour shows the concept, not just memorised labels.

constraints: At 7–8, avoid newton-meters, magnetic-field language and iron filings — keep it exploratory and hands-on.
Do NOT present action-at-a-distance as obvious; if pupils think it is obvious they are missing the point — honour the strangeness as the start of the journey towards fields.
Keep magnetic, gravitational and electrostatic forces separate; note only that they share 'acting at a distance', and do not conflate their terminology or representations.

A tap-to-reveal labelled scene (force names, contact/non-contact badges, lift-the-flap 'do they touch?' answers) is a useful vocabulary and reference layer for this naming-heavy topic, but a fixed image cannot show the gap-spanning force changing, so it supports rather than delivers the core insight.
A sorting or short-choice task checks and consolidates understanding and may teach or check classification, but does not by itself elicit the independent explanation the core activities aim for.
Paper or card used in the gap test has real thickness; this is fine as a physical approximation — the point is that nothing physical has to bridge the gap for a non-contact force to act.
Pair any digital gap-test with real magnets in hand; the tactile pull is part of the learning, not a replacement for it.

Treat the steel-tray result as setup-dependent: a magnetic steel tray is attracted to the magnet and may conduct flux (paperclip clings to the tray) or reduce/block the pull on the paperclip, while non-magnetic paper does neither — test the specific tray and magnet before the lesson.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. The activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Two of the three cited sources are marked verified:false in the source row (the IOP non-contact-forces collection and the ASSIST misconceptions page); treat their claims accordingly and re-verify before relying on them.

The 'remove the air' / vacuum claim (that magnetism works with no medium) is physically sound for these forces, but is demonstrated digitally or by clip here rather than by a direct classroom vacuum experiment — it is an assertion supported by physics, not something the learner directly observes with equipment.

The original recommendation framed a stateful 2D simulation as the only medium that can show the gap-spanning force ('only a stateful 2D sim can show...'). This comparative-necessity claim is not established by the sources; the rewrite presents the live arrows/toggle as one effective mechanism alongside physical magnets and paper tests.

The steel-tray probe is setup-dependent: a ferromagnetic steel tray is itself attracted to the magnet and interacts with it — depending on tray thickness and magnet strength it may conduct flux (the paperclip clings to the tray) or shield/reduce the pull reaching the paperclip. Either way it demonstrates material-specificity, not that steel is transparent to the force; test with the actual equipment before use. Non-magnetic paper does none of this.
Predict-then-test methodology in activity 2 derives from the stored best-practice guidance and POE task, not directly from a cited source claim, so its sourceClaims is left empty.

assess.poeTask: Set a paperclip a small gap from a magnet. Ask the child to predict whether the pull still works (a) with a sheet of paper slipped into the gap and (b) with a steel baking tray slipped in — and WHY. Predicting the paper blocks it reveals contact-thinking; the surprise that paper doesn't but the steel tray does opens up action-at-a-distance and material-specificity.
probeDeeper: Is a push a contact or a non-contact force? What about friction? How do you know?
Would the magnet pull an aluminium can the way it pulls the paperclip? Why does that matter?
If the magnet and paperclip were in a jar with all the air sucked out, what would happen?
assess.correctAnswer: Magnetism is a non-contact force — it acts across a distance, so the magnet and paperclip don't need to touch. This is unlike a push, a pull by hand, or friction, which are contact forces that only work when the objects touch.

errorPatterns.pattern: 'They must really be touching somehow — there's something invisible in the gap joining them.'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Lift the paperclip toward the magnet through a sheet of paper or clear plastic — nothing spans the gap yet the force acts. Name it non-contact.
errorPatterns.distractor: They aren't really apart — something invisible in the gap is touching them together.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Insists on a hidden physical link and won't accept a genuine gap.

errorPatterns.pattern: 'The magnet needs the air to push the paperclip — with no air it wouldn't work.'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Explain (and show or clip) magnets working in a vacuum or under water — the air isn't the go-between.
errorPatterns.distractor: No — the magnet needs air in between to carry the pull across.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Says removing the air would stop the pull.

errorPatterns.pattern: 'Magnetism and gravity are the same invisible pulling force.'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Contrast: gravity pulls ANY object and only attracts; magnetism pulls only iron/steel-type materials and can also repel.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: When sorting, groups gravity with magnetism as identical, or says the magnet pulls 'like gravity'.

responseLevels.gap: Denies a real gap ('they're secretly touching') or says the air carries the force; cannot separate contact from non-contact.
responseLevels.full: Explains that contact forces need the objects to touch while non-contact forces (magnetism, and later gravity) act across a distance with no contact or medium, sorts a novel example correctly, and can say why a vacuum wouldn't stop a magnet.
responseLevels.partial: Correctly sorts pushes and friction as contact and magnetism as non-contact, but only matches examples to categories — lists them without explaining that a non-contact force acts across a gap with no medium needed, or still ties it to air.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: A magnet pulls a paperclip toward it across a small gap, without ever touching it. How can the magnet pull the paperclip when nothing is touching it?
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who grasps the distinction accepts that a force can act across a gap and names magnetism as non-contact. A child holding 'forces must involve touching' invents an invisible connector ('tiny hairs', 'they're secretly touching') or claims the air carries the pull (so it would fail in a vacuum). The mechanism they invoke reveals whether action-at-a-distance is accepted.
